title_original: The Bicentenary of Photography – Drawing Lab: Eclipse

blocks.text: On the occasion of the Bicentennial of Photography, the group exhibition Eclipse explores the relationship between photography and drawing at the Drawing Lab — a venue dedicated to the experimentation and promotion of contemporary drawing, located at 17 rue de Richelieu, 75001 Paris. Through graphic focalisations, perceptual blurring and photosensitive devices, drawing, in all its dimensions, emerges in the shadow of photography, revealing its materiality, its uses, and the very processes through which images come into being. The exhibition brings together emblematic works, recent pieces and new interactive installations.

Featuring works of Fabienne Ballandras, Léa Belooussovitch, Mireille Blanc, Nicolas Daubanes, Jean Olivier Hucleux, Éric Manigaud, Célia Muller, Daphné Nan Le Sergent, Pascal Navarro and Jérémie Setton.
Curated by Anne Favier. Exhibition on view from 25 September 2026 to 3 January 2027.

While Nicéphore Niépce invented photographic image-making in 1826, his contemporary Henry Fox Talbot also believed he had discovered, through photography, a “faithful pencil” capable of naturally capturing the writing of shadows and light. He likewise referred to photograms, light- sensitive impressions obtained through direct contact, as “photogenic drawings”, early manifestationsof photography as a process of fixing and momentarily obscuring light.

Today, photography is recognised as one of the major artistic mediums. This group exhibition seeks to highlight the close dialogue it maintains with contemporary drawing in all its forms, and to show how drawing continues to develop and reinvent itself in the shadow of this two-hundred-year- old invention.

At a time when photography and post-photography generate the vast majority of images, some artists working with drawing maintain a striking proximity to photographic source-images, sometimes reproducing or translating them with remarkable fidelity. In doing so, they create drawings of extraordinary photogenic quality, prompting viewers to question whether they are looking at a graphic or photographic image. But why spend so much time redrawing a snapshot? The transfer of a photographic image into drawing is above all a process of revelation: the document becomes a surface to be scrutinised, excavated and transformed—“transmuted”, in the words of Jean Olivier Hucleux. While the draughtsperson tends to efface themselves in the act of reproducing the image, they simultaneously reveal and intensify the traces of the photographic—detail, grain, texture, surface, materiality and fragility—while endowing the image with a new sense of duration and tactility. Through a historical work by Jean Olivier Hucleux and more recent works by Daphné Nan Le Sergent, Mireille Blanc, Éric Manigaud and Célia Muller, the exhibition seeks to make tangible this “graphite becoming of the image”, to borrow Jean-Christophe Bailly’s expression for the passage into drawing.

The photographic image may also eclipse itself through various processes of graphic transposition: blurring (Léa Belooussovitch), “blind” transcription, superimposition, association or juxtaposition (Fabienne Ballandras). These visual shifts generate new focal adjustments and viewing distances, perceptual disruptions—sometimes leading to illegibility or abstraction—and open up critical perspectives on photographic images, particularly those circulated by the media, from iconic press photographs to the captions that accompany them. Drawing thus grants these images new materialities, visibilities and temporalities.

By presenting complex photo-graphic devices, Nicolas Daubanes’s incandescent photograms, an interactive installation by Jérémie Setton in which the viewer plays a double role in revealing the image, and Pascal Navarro’s photosensitive works that gradually emerge over time—the exhibition also explores, through drawing, the founding principles of photography: the latent image,development, fixation, reproducibility, the reversibility of negative and positive, photosensitisation and imprint. Through these experimental works, drawing itself becomes photographic.

A historical work, emblematic and experimental pieces, newly commissioned productions and installations reactivated for the Drawing Lab come together to form a dialogue across three thematic sections — “Graphite Becoming”, “Focal Adjustments” and “Latent Image”. Through these resonances, Eclipse reveals drawing as it is tested, transformed and redefined through itsencounter with photography.
